bus_p3_r2: Your Protector (I know, almost the same name, but this one's the grown-up you) earns that protective part's trust mostly out in ordinary life. That part wants to see you actually do stuff, for a good while, before it believes a trustworthy adult has shown up. One kind talk in your head usually won't outweigh years of evidence the other way, and I don't think it should. The things you do can be small, like keeping a promise to yourself nobody else knew about. Or saying no to someone, and not texting an hour later to take it back. That second one can be really hard.
bus_p4_r2: That part doesn't have to leave first. You could even tell it, "Stay right there if you want." It can watch the whole time while you try one small step, as long as you stay present and could stop if you needed to. And if it says no? Then it's no. When it does let you go on, follow whatever changes. A critic that kept saying "This is stupid" might soften into "I'm scared to get my hopes up." That one's easier to be kind to.
bus_p5_r2: No need to restart the whole exercise and go looking for your little one again, like they're hiding behind the couch. Maybe a vague hurt turns out to be about wanting someone on your side for once. Oof. If it does, try being that someone. You could even say it out loud: "I'm on your side." It may feel silly to say out loud. Notice how it lands anyway. You don't need to know how old you were, or what happened, to do that. A small shift counts, and more intensity isn't the only way forward. Sometimes all that happens is your shoulders come down a little.
